subject: Genetics and biochemistry: Punnett squares, Hardy-Weinberg, pedigree, Michaelis-Menten kinetics

items.answer: Gametes T and t from each parent; the square contains TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Genotype ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotype ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf (75 % tall, 25 % dwarf).
items.method: Fill the 2x2 Punnett square with the combined gametes and count genotypes and phenotypes.

items.answer: The tall parent is heterozygous, Tt: Tt x tt gives 1/2 Tt (tall) and 1/2 tt (dwarf). A TT parent would give only tall offspring.
items.method: Test cross: a 1:1 ratio reveals a heterozygous parent.

items.answer: Wrinkled and green is rryy: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16. Round and yellow (R_ Y_): 3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16.
items.method: Independent assortment: multiply the monohybrid probabilities (dihybrid ratio 9:3:3:1).

items.answer: Rr x Rr gives 1/2 Rr and Yy x Yy gives 1/2 Yy, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 (4/16) of the offspring are RrYy.
items.method: Multiply the heterozygote probabilities for the two independent genes.
The recessive phenotype frequency equals q^2 in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

items.answer: p = 1 - q = 0.60. Expected genotype frequencies: AA = p^2 = 0.36, Aa = 2pq = 0.48, aa = q^2 = 0.16 (sum 1.00).

items.method: Multiply the frequency 2pq by the population size.

items.answer: Any two of: random mating, very large population (no genetic drift), no natural selection on the locus, no mutation, no migration (gene flow).
items.method: Recall the assumptions of the Hardy-Weinberg principle.

items.answer: Recessive. The unaffected parents I-1 and I-2 have an affected daughter (II-1); the trait skipped a generation in them, which is impossible for a dominant trait (an affected child of a dominant trait needs an affected parent).
items.method: Two unaffected parents with an affected child imply a recessive allele.

items.answer: Autosomal. For an X-linked recessive trait an affected daughter (II-1) must receive an X with the allele from her father, who would then be affected, but I-1 is unaffected. So the trait is autosomal recessive.
items.method: Check whether the pedigree is compatible with X-linked inheritance: a father passes his X to every daughter.

items.answer: (i) I-1 = Aa and I-2 = Aa (both carriers, since they have an affected aa child). (ii) II-1 = aa (affected, homozygous recessive). (iii) II-3 = Aa and II-4 = Aa: both are unaffected but have an affected son III-1 (aa), so each parent passed on an a allele.
items.method: Sub-parts (i) to (iii) answered together: unaffected parents of an aa child must each carry one a allele; affected individuals of a recessive trait are aa; an affected child of unaffected parents makes both parents obligate carriers.

items.answer: III-2 is unaffected, so she is AA or Aa with the offspring ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa of Aa x Aa; the probability that she is a carrier is 2/3 (about 0.67).
items.method: Conditional probability: exclude the aa outcome from the Punnett square of two carriers.

items.answer: Vmax is about 80 umol/min (the plateau the curve approaches; accept roughly 75 to 85). Km is the substrate concentration at half of Vmax: v = 40 umol/min at [S] = 4 mM, so Km is about 4 mM.
items.method: Vmax from the saturation level, Km from the [S] at which v = Vmax/2.
Insert [S] = 12 mM, Vmax = 80 umol/min and Km = 4 mM into the Michaelis-Menten equation.
Set v = 0.9 Vmax and solve for [S].

items.answer: A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Km (more substrate is needed to reach Vmax/2) while Vmax stays the same. The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site, so a large [S] outcompetes the inhibitor and the enzyme can still reach Vmax.
items.method: Conceptual: competitive inhibition changes Km,app = Km (1 + [I]/Ki) but not Vmax.
